text: Defaults differ by database: MySQL's InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, while PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED. Neither defaults to SERIALIZABLE.
why: The same booking code can behave differently on MySQL and PostgreSQL; readers should know which default they are on.

text: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE does not queue transactions. It runs them concurrently and aborts one with a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001) when the result could differ from a serial order, so applications 'must be prepared to retry transactions due to serialization failures'.
why: Corrects the 'one after another' mental model and tells the reader the practical cost: retry logic.

text: In MySQL InnoDB, SERIALIZABLE is REPEATABLE READ plus one change: plain SELECTs are implicitly turned into SELECT ... FOR SHARE when autocommit is disabled. Two transactions that both read a seat and then try to update it can therefore deadlock.
why: Shows how serializability is actually enforced in the lecture's database (MySQL) and why it is slow.

text: MySQL defines SELECT ... FOR UPDATE as locking rows 'the same as if you issued an UPDATE statement for those rows'. An UPDATE ... WHERE sets an exclusive lock on every record its search encounters, so an UPDATE is always a locking operation.
why: Fixes the belief that a plain UPDATE takes no row lock.

text: In PostgreSQL READ COMMITTED, a second UPDATE of a row that another transaction is updating waits for it to commit, then re-checks its WHERE clause against the new row version before applying. Under REPEATABLE READ the same situation aborts with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update', and the transaction must be retried.
why: This is exactly the 'what happens to a plain UPDATE' question the student asked; it explains why a conditional UPDATE (WHERE seat is still free) is safe.

text: PostgreSQL warns that 'The rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server; therefore a large OFFSET might be inefficient.' This is why deep pages of LIMIT/OFFSET pagination get slower and keyset (cursor) pagination is preferred.
why: The true part of the teacher's point, stated precisely.

text: MySQL stops early on LIMIT when it can: with ORDER BY on an index it reads only the first rows, but if a filesort is needed, 'all rows that match the query without the LIMIT clause are selected, and most or all of them are sorted' before the first rows are returned.
why: Shows when LIMIT saves disk reads (index order) and when it doesn't (filesort).

text: In MySQL, what is flushed at commit is the redo log. With the default innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1, 'Logs are written and flushed to disk at each transaction commit'. Settings 0 and 2 flush about once per second, and unflushed transactions 'can be lost in a crash'.
why: Durability is a configuration choice; readers tuning for throughput need to know what they give up.

text: InnoDB 'does not physically remove a row from the database immediately when you delete it'. The row is delete-marked and later physically removed by a background purge, once no transaction needs it for MVCC or rollback.
why: Gives the documented mechanism behind 'databases soft-delete then batch-clean'.

text: In PostgreSQL, an UPDATE or DELETE leaves the old row version in place because it 'must not be deleted while it is still potentially visible to other transactions'. VACUUM later removes these dead row versions and marks the space for reuse.
why: Same pattern in the other major open-source RDBMS; links soft-delete-then-clean to MVCC.

text: DynamoDB's TTL feature deletes expired items in the background, 'typically within a few days after their expiration', without consuming write throughput. Until then expired items can still be returned, so queries should filter them out.
why: This is the real deferred-deletion feature in DynamoDB and mirrors the lecture's expiry-based KV store design.

text: SQL:2011 system-versioned temporal tables (for example SQL Server 2016+) offer opt-in, built-in history: on DELETE 'The system stores the previous value of the row in the history table', and the row disappears from normal queries but can still be read with FOR SYSTEM_TIME.
why: The closest built-in relational feature to soft delete; useful for audit and recovery.

text: The building blocks named here have sharp edges. MySQL says SKIP LOCKED queries 'return an inconsistent view of the data' and are 'not suitable for general transactional work', but they suit queue-like tables. NOWAIT fails immediately with an error instead of waiting for a locked row.
why: Readers who use these primitives need to know their intended use.

text: Django's CONN_MAX_AGE defaults to 0, which closes the database connection at the end of each request. Native connection pooling for PostgreSQL (OPTIONS 'pool' with psycopg) only arrived in Django 5.1.
why: A concrete, current example behind the connection-pooling complaint, and the fix.

text: Not every ORM is weak at pooling: SQLAlchemy's Engine 'has a QueuePool integrated, pre-configured with reasonable pooling defaults' (pool size 5).
why: Keeps the reader from generalising one ORM's default to all.

text: Django lets you load only some columns: only() loads just the named fields and defer() skips the named ones (a deferred field is fetched on first access, one query per field). values() returns plain dicts instead of model instances.
why: Shows the projection is available, and its trap (lazy deferred loads).

text: A classic ORM performance trap is the N+1 query pattern, where touching a related object in a loop fires one query per row. Django's select_related (a JOIN) and prefetch_related (one batched query) are 'designed to stop the deluge of database queries that is caused by accessing related objects'.
why: The most common concrete reason ORM queries are non-optimal.

text: Django can call a stored procedure directly with cursor.callproc(name, params), and can map raw SQL results onto model instances with Manager.raw().
why: Gives the practical escape hatch for the optimized-stored-procedure case.

text: Vitess is 'an open-source database clustering system for horizontal scaling of MySQL' through sharding, and it 'served all YouTube database traffic for over five years'.
why: A well-known public example backing 'relational databases do scale'.

text: In Codd's model a relation is 'a set of tuples', using the term in its mathematical sense. In SQL, 'relations are represented by tables', with each row a tuple.
why: Gives the actual origin of the word 'relational'.
